claims.text: The starting material is a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar colony microstructure.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal lamellar or colony boundaries generate local stress concentrations.
The boundary stress concentrations promote premature microcracking and brittle failure.
The proposed intervention is a minor dopant addition, such as boron, combined with a short controlled anneal.
The anneal should be conducted under an inert atmosphere at approximately 0.3–0.5 Tm.
Dopant-assisted annealing will cause selective dopant segregation at internal dual-phase lamellar boundaries.
Optimizing annealing duration can produce interfacial segregation without bulk microstructural coarsening.
Boundary-segregated dopant improves interface cohesion by reducing interfacial misfit.
Dopant segregation reduces the barrier to dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
Improved dislocation transmission reduces dislocation pile-ups at lamellar boundaries.
Reduced dislocation pile-ups lower local boundary stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations limit microcrack initiation and promote more uniform plastic deformation.
The treatment will significantly increase room-temperature strain-to-failure relative to the untreated alloy.
The treatment will retain or slightly increase room-temperature tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
Treated specimens will exhibit fewer dislocation pile-ups and fewer microcrack-initiation sites than untreated specimens.
Excess dopant or nonoptimal annealing may form coarse precipitates or cause embrittlement.
